passage:
Sonali: going to Heena's birthday tonight, back by 10
Mohit: again? u were out last week
Sonali: that was my cousin's thing
Mohit: if u go, don't bother texting me after. i'm done
Sonali: Mohit please. it's two hours
Mohit: and maybe everyone should see what u said about Heena in our chats
Sonali: you'd show her??
Mohit: ur choice
Sonali sat on the edge of her bed in her going-out kurta, the gift bag beside her. She pictured Mohit hurt and alone. She pictured Heena reading those old messages. She could no longer tell whether staying home was her decision.
Sonali: ok. i won't go
Mohit: good. see, i just care about u
She took off her earrings and texted Heena that she had a headache. It was the third excuse that month.

qa.q: Whose birthday was Sonali planning to go to?
qa.a: Sonali was planning to go to Heena's birthday.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling as she sat on the bed?
qa.a: She felt pity for Mohit and fear of the old messages being shown, so torn that she could not tell whether staying home was her own decision.

qa.q: What protective step could Sonali take instead of texting an excuse?
qa.a: She could save the threatening messages, tell someone she trusts what is happening, and contact a helpline for support if the threats continue.

qa.q: What would change if Mohit had replied "okay, have fun"?
qa.a: Sonali could go without fear, and her choices would be her own instead of being steered by threats of leaving and exposure.

grounding: A young woman gives up Heena's birthday after threats of being left and of old chats being shown, feeling pity and fear and losing track of her own choice.

passage:
Every evening after college, Gargi walked the dusty road past the temple tank to Damini's house, even on days she had tests.
It had started in spring, when Gargi mentioned applying for a nursing course in the city. Damini went white. "You'll forget me. If you leave, I'll tell your father you've been meeting that boy from the bus stand." There was no boy. Gargi had spoken to him once, about bus timings. But in this town, a rumour would be enough.
So Gargi didn't send the form. She stopped going to the library with the other girls, because Damini called that choosing them. When Damini cried, Gargi comforted her; when Damini smiled, Gargi felt safe for a day.
Tonight, walking home under the neem trees, she wondered which of her choices this year had actually been hers.
The nursing form was still folded in her bag.

qa.q: What course did Gargi want to apply for?
qa.a: Gargi wanted to apply for a nursing course in the city.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling on the walk home under the neem trees?
qa.a: She felt confused and trapped, unsure which of her choices that year had really been her own.

qa.q: What could Gargi do with the folded nursing form?
qa.a: She could quietly talk to a trusted adult, such as a teacher or relative, about the threat and her plans, and get help sending the form rather than letting fear decide.

qa.q: How might Damini be feeling behind the threats?
qa.a: Damini seems terrified of being forgotten, but turning that fear into threats traps Gargi instead of keeping her close.

grounding: A young woman in a small town gives up an application and outings after a threat of a false rumour, caught between pity and fear of what might follow.

passage:
"Harish, why aren't you going to Pune? The internship's paid. You were so excited," Ujjwal said, sitting on the edge of the hostel bed.
"Riya said if I go, she'll post our old chats online. The private ones."
"What?"
"And she cried. She said she'll have nobody. I feel so bad for her. And also… I'm scared of her."
"So you're giving up the internship."
"I don't know if it's me choosing or her. I can't tell anymore."
Ujjwal was quiet. Then: "Threatening to post private chats isn't love. It's a threat. And you can report that."
"She'd hate me."
"Harish, you're allowed to go to Pune. Let's talk to the college counsellor tomorrow morning. And tonight, let's save screenshots of what she said, just in case."
Harish let out a long breath. "Okay. Tomorrow. Come with me?"
"I'll come."

qa.q: What did Riya threaten to post online?
qa.a: Our old chats. The private ones.

qa.q: How does Harish feel about Riya's threats?
qa.a: Harish feels both pity and fear: sorry for her crying, but scared of her and unsure whether the choice is Harish's own.

qa.q: What steps does Ujjwal suggest?
qa.a: Ujjwal suggests saving screenshots of the threats and going to the college counsellor the next morning, and offers to go along.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see Riya's behaviour?
qa.a: Ujjwal sees the threat to post private chats as coercion, not love, and something that can be reported.

grounding: It shows a young adult giving up a paid internship because a partner threatens exposure, torn between pity and fear.

passage:
I'm Himani, and for most of second year I lived around Usha's moods.
Whenever I made plans with anyone else, dance practice, a cousin's wedding, even a study group, Usha would say something like, "Fine. But then don't expect me to keep quiet about your family's problems." My parents' fights were the one secret I'd told her.
Or she'd cry and say, "You're all I have. If you leave me, I'll have nothing."
I felt terribly sorry for her. I was also scared. So I dropped dance. I skipped the wedding. I stopped answering other friends.
The worst part was that I didn't know anymore which things I wanted and which things I was doing so she wouldn't explode or tell.
It was my cousin who finally said, "Himani, you're shrinking." I started seeing the college counsellor after that. Slowly, I got my own choices back.

qa.q: What did Himani drop because of Usha's threats?
qa.a: Himani dropped dance.

qa.q: How did Himani feel about Usha during second year?
qa.a: Himani felt deeply sorry for Usha and also scared, unable to tell which choices were really Himani's own.

qa.q: What helped Himani start getting her choices back?
qa.a: Himani's cousin named what was happening, and Himani began seeing the college counsellor.

qa.q: How did Himani's cousin see what was happening?
qa.a: The cousin saw Himani shrinking, giving up so much, and was worried enough to say so.

grounding: A young adult recalls giving up dance, a wedding and friendships under a friend's threats of exposure and loss, feeling pity and fear at once.

passage:
Student counsellor's note, Thursday.
Tarun came in this afternoon, exhausted. He wants to move out of his shared room, but his roommate, Yogesh, has said, "If you leave, I'll hurt myself, and it'll be your fault."
Tarun has cancelled two trips home and stopped going to his cricket practice to stay with Yogesh in the evenings. He said, "I feel so sorry for him. And I'm terrified. I don't know whose life I'm living."
I told Tarun that a threat like this must always be taken seriously, and that it is not his job to carry it alone or give up his own life because of it.
With his agreement, I contacted the hostel warden straight away. The warden went to check on Yogesh within the hour, and our team called Yogesh in for support this evening. I have also arranged a room change for Tarun, and we will meet again on Monday.

qa.q: What did Tarun stop going to?
qa.a: His cricket practice.

qa.q: How does Tarun feel about Yogesh's threat?
qa.a: Tarun feels both sorry for Yogesh and terrified, unsure whose life he is living.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do the same day?
qa.a: The counsellor contacted the hostel warden straight away, who checked on Yogesh within the hour, and the team called Yogesh in for support that evening.

qa.q: How might Yogesh be feeling behind the threat?
qa.a: Yogesh is probably very frightened of being left alone, which needs real support rather than Tarun staying out of fear.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young adult trapped by a roommate's self-harm threat, and passes the threat to help the same day while freeing the student.

passage:
Tuesday night
Skipped Rakesh's birthday again. Third plan this month. Gautam said if I went, he'd finally tell my parents about the backlog paper and move out, and then who'd split the rent? When I said no to him last month, he didn't talk for days and then cried that I'm the only one he has.
And I believe him, that's the thing. I feel sorry for him. He really doesn't have many people. But I'm also scared every time my phone lights up.
I can't tell anymore which things I want and which things I do so he won't explode. Do I even still like badminton, or did I stop because he hated me going?
Tonight I called Anu-di and told her everything. She was quiet, then said, "This isn't your fault, and his threats aren't yours to fix. Let's go to your college counsellor together on Thursday." I feel lighter than I have in weeks.
Naveen

qa.q: Whose birthday did Naveen skip?
qa.a: Rakesh's birthday.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Naveen have about Gautam?
qa.a: Naveen feels sorry for Gautam, who doesn't have many people, and scared every time the phone lights up, which blurs where Naveen's own choices end.

qa.q: Why was calling Anu-di a good step?
qa.a: Telling a trusted person broke the isolation; Anu-di said it wasn't Naveen's fault and planned a visit to the college counsellor together.

qa.q: How does Anu-di respond to what Naveen shares?
qa.a: Anu-di takes it seriously, says it isn't Naveen's fault and the threats aren't Naveen's to fix, and offers to go to the counsellor together.

grounding: Shows a young adult giving up friends and plans because saying no brings threats of exposure and loss, feeling both pity and fear.
